oral_history_corpus.description: Hi, it's Mike with UGtastic . I'm here at GOTO Conference 2015, and I'm sitting here with Vyacheslav Egorov, who gave a talk on benchmarking JS. Hi, it's Mike with UGtastic . I'm here at GOTO Conference 2015, and I'm sitting here with Vyacheslav Egorov, who gave a talk on benchmarking JS. JavaScript performance is a critical aspect of web development. Vyacheslav Egorov explains why many benchmarks are incorrect and provides insights into optimizing your JavaScript code.
oral_history_corpus.transcript_text: Hi, it's Mike with UGtastic . I'm here at GOTO Conference 2015, and I'm sitting here with Vyacheslav Egorov, who gave a talk on benchmarking JS. Thank you very much for taking the time to speak with me. When you talk about benchmarking JS, are you talking about client-side JS? I mean, JS lives in a lot of different places. Is this Node? Is this browser JS? What are you benchmarking? So, I don't have any particular focus. I'm just looking at the pure JavaScript performance. So, it doesn't matter if you run your JavaScript on the client-side or server-side. Basically, no matter where you are, my talk applies to you. Okay. So, you know, even if I'm in V8 or Rhino or whatever, it's going to be... Okay, so, when you talk, what techniques and tools were you talking about? Where did this talk come from? What experiences did you have that led you to this? Well, I used to work on the V8 team, and when you work on a team of the VM engineers, you usually get different questions from the users, in this case, JavaScript developers, who don't completely understand what happens inside the VM and how they should measure performance of their code. And that's what this talk is based on. Basically, I monitor different social media, and I see people posting different benchmarks, and I look what happens there, and I explain why these benchmarks are usually incorrect. And that's, yeah, that's basically my experience. So, what are some of the things that you see that are incorrect, and like, what are some quick tips, or articles people should read or try to understand better about JavaScript performance? I think the biggest issue is that people still think that JavaScript implementations are very dumb, but these implementations are quite smart. So, I think that that's the main thing that they should know about that, and they should always account for the very advanced optimizations that the JS engines are capable of doing now. So, there is no really single tip. They should just try to understand what is happening on the inside. Okay. Now, if you're dealing with V8 optimization, one of the things is that JavaScript runs anywhere, on V8, Rhino, different browsers. Does the wisdom of "this is good for JavaScript performance" apply generally everywhere? Or do you find people benchmarking on V8, and then when they try a different VM they see very different performance characteristics? Sometimes that happens, but these days, the implementations really converge on, they apply the same techniques, so it's quite often that you see the same performance characteristics across all of the platforms you use. That's why this talk is quite universal, and this issue is quite universal. Okay, and when you're looking at the way JavaScript is being implemented, I mean, I've heard people on Twitter tweeting about, you know, if you're trying to implement a class structure in JavaScript, don't reimplement the classical inheritance structure, use the prototypal inheritance and different ways of structuring your application. Does that play into the way people reason about writing JavaScript, and its performance? If I'm implementing a class in JavaScript, is that generally gonna perform worse or better than if I do something more native? So the thing is that JavaScript engines evolve naturally, so they follow the paths that people are using, so they optimize for the patterns that people are using. In this sense, if you use, for example, constructors and prototypes, this is actually the most performant way of writing JavaScript, especially if you keep everything, like, kind of static. Yeah, you just follow the common patterns and then you will be safe. Okay, and as far as working on the V8 engine itself, I didn't realize it before our conversation. How did you get involved in working on V8, which has become something of an industry change? Not just with Chrome, but with Node being built on that. You're working on some pretty intense technology. So, well, I stopped working on V8 three years ago, but I was doing the Java VM before back in Russia, and then V8 people were searching for a person with a compiler background, and they hired me, so I joined the team. I worked on different parts of V8, from garbage collection to compiler infrastructure. So I have the background in this, and that background seems to fit with what the team needed. Right. Okay, you described two things earlier. One is that JavaScript implementations are much smarter than people give them credit for, and that the current patterns of how people write their applications are being used to derive how these JS VMs work. Is there something, a common pattern that people are using, that you kind of wish they would just move away from? Like, even though we have classical class and inheritance, but if they wrote their JavaScript a different way, it would be a lot more efficient? And they might get a lot more native, and they might get a lot more benefits that they don't see now. Is there anything, any advice or observations you've made? No, I actually have an opposite issue. So, the, the JavaScript VMs, even though they are quite smart, they still, because they evolve by following what people do, they are very focused. So, what I really want them to do is to start expanding this area of fast JavaScript and support, like, different corners of the language they do not support well, or they just fall to the slow path, and so on. So, it's actually the other way around. Not the people. Well, no, you're saying you wish they would do more of, be aware of these other types of structures? Yes, exactly. Yeah. Yeah. So you are a little bit frustrated with it, like, "Hey, we're just going to do this one type of structure, but JavaScript is so much more than that." Precisely. Okay, great. Well, thank you very much for taking the time to speak with me. Thank you. I appreciate it. All right, thank you.

oral_history_corpus.title: Sarah Allen & Desi McAdam on RailsBridge Workshops and Education | UGtastic Archive
oral_history_corpus.description: Hi, I'm Mike with UGtastic here again at SCNA. I'm sitting down with Sarah Allen and Desi McAdam. Hi, I'm Mike with UGtastic here again at SCNA. I'm sitting down with Sarah Allen and Desi McAdam.
oral_history_corpus.transcript_text: Hi, I'm Mike with UGtastic here again at SCNA. I'm sitting down with Sarah Allen and Desi McAdam. They created the RailsBridge Workshop, which is, well, I'll let you describe what exactly is the RailsBridge Workshop. So, RailsBridge is a broad organization that was started by a number of Rails developers who really wanted to create the kind of community that they wanted to be a part of. Sarah May and myself started what's, as the RailsBridge Project, it's the RailsBridge Open Workshops. And specifically in San Francisco, we used the Open Workshop formula to create outreach workshops to women. And the idea is we're using open source practices to apply to event organization and outreach projects. So, the, what we call recipes or cookbook for creating the event, as well as the curricula, are all open source and freely available for anybody to use for anything. And then Desi has happened to be traveling all over the world and has created instances of these workshops wherever she's been, as well as dozens or many, many, many other volunteers have done that all over the country and the world. What's the format? What is, what is it, what is it, what the current, because you said it's an open source thing, so I'm sure there's some evolution. What is the current format of a... So, the core format is a Friday night, Saturday event, where on Friday, all of the installation occurs. So, you have volunteers who come and help people get their machines set up because that is often the most difficult part for beginners. And it really has nothing to do with the, you know, writing code or dueling. It can be a wall. The particular technology. Or your Ruby on my computer, boom. Yeah, I mean, particularly Rails is so many collections of open source packages and it's particularly hard on, you know, and it's different for each machine you're on. Once you've got Ruby and Rails installed, it's easy. And then it's different for the different technologies and, in fact, there's now a front-end workshop that doesn't have an evening install fest because everybody has a browser and a text editor. Yeah, that's, yeah, that one's... But, but for the Rails workshop, that is really an important step. And then Saturday is everybody follows the same curricula and you have at least two groups. One is for people who've never written code before and the other is for, you know, whatever degree of experience. Maybe they already hit Java but they never did Rails. Exactly. So, sometimes we'll find that people who are sysadmins are faster learning Rails than experienced programmers who maybe have done desktop applications but aren't very familiar with the command line. So, your level of experience as a coder doesn't necessarily correlate to how fast you'll learn the very first steps of Rails. So, you might have predisposed towards, oh, this is how we do it on the desktop, whereas somebody who's maybe had some scripting experience doesn't have maybe as rigorous a mindset on, oh, yeah, it has to be this way. Yeah, because you'll have different learning curves for people who've done web apps, so they understand HTTP, versus people who've done C++, therefore they understand object-oriented programming, versus people who've done a lot of command line stuff, and so they're very facile with the scripting aspects of it. So, we try to group people into like-minded experience, but mostly, it's depending on the size of the workshop, the grouping is flexible, depending on the venue and the size and the number of volunteers and teachers you have. And sometimes it's just everybody's in a room and we figure it out. Yeah. And does, you, you, or you wanted to say something? Yeah, I was just going to say, in addition to that, so like, typically I try to, I try to group people based on very broad generalizations, so I've, I've programmed before, I've never programmed before, or I've done some Rails, but I need some more help with, you know, more advanced concepts. And then split the people apart and try to get the TAs that match sort of those, like, comfort levels of teaching. And you said you've gone all over the world and done these all over. I'm just curious, like, all, I mean, literally, like, when you say world, what do you mean? Well, so I've done them, so I've done one, I've done quite a few in the United States, and I've done one in Singapore, and I've helped out with one in Chile, and I can't remember every world. But it's really easy to, once you've seen one run and you have a desire to do them, it's really not very difficult if you, you know, ping the mailing list. Everybody will tell you what the latest, you know, we just ran one last weekend, and this is what we ran into. We've already done pool requests to update the documentation, you know, et cetera, et cetera. So everybody's super helpful. And there's some really nice side effects that come from that. A lot of people who don't really know anything about the workshops go to our instructions for how to install rails, because, you know, a new version of this or that comes out, and the install instructions change. But because now there are workshops happening several times a month in lots of different places, those are updated by the volunteers, and there are different volunteers every time, so it isn't as much of a burden. So it's also kind of becoming a documentation unto itself, not just a script for how to do these classes, but also, hey, I just need to set up rails. How do I do that? Yes. Yeah, there's a lot of different things that come out of it, and, you know, educational resources and set up resources and different things. So that's a pretty neat side effect of the community. And I do want to ask about the social aspect. The way I understand is that the legend is that Sarah Ellen and Sarah May were at a conference, and they didn't see a lot of other women. Did you realize that you were the only two women and hundreds of people? And you wanted to create something that would help bring... Yeah, so the stats are there. We were at a conference where there were 200 people and six women. So that's 3%, which is reflective of... Or is it 2%? Well, in any case, it's around the number of women in open source, which is much, much smaller than the number of women in the corporate world doing programming. And I came more from companies which were less involved with open source, where I felt that there were not very many women, but there were more women than I saw in the Ruby community. And I'd been meaning to learn Ruby for three years before I had started learning Ruby in 2008. And so I thought, and I still believe it's true, that there are more women programmers in the Bay Area than there are Ruby programmers. Really? Therefore, if there's 20% of programmers are women, overall, statistically... Why aren't 20% of Ruby developers? No, it's actually more... we have a bigger opportunity than that. Oh, okay. Because Ruby is a small language. So therefore, if we just convert some of the existing programmers to no Ruby, then it would be easy to actually get 50%. And in any of the new languages, I think we have a real big opportunity to do that. Because in any specific community, we can change the ratio much easier because it's smaller than just, you know, the boiling the ocean problem. And I also heard that in the startups, it's also a boys club culture as well. And with Ginny, I did an interview with Ginny a few months ago, and she described it as when a startup happens, it's usually some friends. They get together and they start the startup, and then they hire people like them from their own network. Is that something that you've seen in the startup world where it tends to be male-dominated companies just... Well, statistically, tech founders are 2% to 3% women. And I think that a lot of that, there is a culture in the United States that is where men have the networks, and men see those kinds of opportunities as available to them for whatever reason. But I do think that the social dynamics of creating situations where women and men and people of all colors and creeds can get together and learn together, then we force those networks where, by example, people see that what you happen to look like, the words you use, your background, doesn't dictate that you are more or less capable of doing these technical things. And when somebody walks into a RailsBridge workshop, they can't tell by looking at somebody whether they're an expert programmer or very successful in their career or unemployed, and all of these things are not correlated with each other and they're not correlated with how to look. And so that's really exciting to me that I hope it will bring that change broadly, but in any case, we are seeing it as absolutely making those changes in pockets. And I think that we need to overcome this problem one person at a time, one mentor at a time. Climate seats all over so that way eventually these communities can... Well, I think that we're talking about changing the ratio is a boil-in-the-ocean kind of problem. However, since we've proven that this template can be fairly easily reproduced by anyone, I like to think that we can boil the ocean by making every tenth molecule a heater. Okay, so basically planting the seeds so that way it can at least distribute these ideas beyond a small community and basically... Yeah, and we're seeing this happen in Ruby, JavaScript, Python, Scala... Oh yeah, so are all of these RailsBridge... well, RailsBridge is, by definition, Rails-oriented, but have you done these for... Well, RailsBridge was created... the name Rails was a little controversial when we were naming it, but we felt that it was coming out of Rails developers, but the Teaching Kids project has always taught... has never taught Rails. Right, yes. However, the Python folks felt like it would alienate their community to call it RailsBridge, so they called it PyStar, because there was already a PyBridge something. But now we're creating an umbrella organization that will be able to support all of these different things. Okay, so that way you don't have to bias that, "Well, I don't want to do that, I don't like Rails. " Yeah. It's... do you have a... well, I won't make you say the name now, because I'm sure it might change, but it's recognizing the fact that we're software developers, not Rails. Yeah, and I think most of us are doing Rails right now. Yeah. Right. And five years from now, we'll be doing something else. Yeah, right now being the operative word there, it's... it might change. Everything changes. And, uh, um, with... with going into a conference, and have you... have you been seeing, uh, since you've started doing this, more women at conferences and more diversity? I mean, SCNA, I think, is an excellent conference. I have. I've noticed a big difference, actually. Yeah, and I think that part of it is that the women in the... some women in the community who weren't coming out to events because they felt alienated have started to come out more. And then the, um, new people in the community have connections to people already in the community. The other thing that has happened in parallel is a lot of the event organizers have realized that they need to take, um, initiative to change how they ask for speakers to create a diversity amongst speakers. And if we have more women speakers, then it's less alienating to, um, have... for women to come to the event. They... they feel like there are role models and mentors for them. And it's easier to look at a group of 20 people. And if you see yourself represented, then you feel like, "Hey, that could be me. " Recently, I learned about a picture that was, uh, uh, very popular in the Obama administration. Uh, when Obama first took office, he was meeting with some... some people, and there were some children there. I'm not exactly sure the context why they were there. But one of the little boys, he was black, and he just said very partly, he said... He asked this question, and they couldn't hear what he said, and they asked him to speak up. And he said, "I want to... I just want to know if your hair feels like mine. " And... and they're... the... the photographer got this amazing picture that was very candid. And it was the president leaning down, and this little boy touching his head. And... what was so inspiring about that is that it was... Here's this generation now seeing somebody like them in... in a position of... of authority and responsibility. And... and are... are you saying that seeing women speaking and running these conferences, running these organizations, says to the women, "There's people like you doing this. " Yeah, I think that there is this myth in our industry that there are no women. Right. That somehow women are less interested or less capable because, as evidenced by there being so few. And I've talked to women who've been the only woman in their company, and then they start to say, "Well, that's just the way the industry is. " Especially if you've been through two jobs like that. But the truth is, numbers-wise, there's tons of amazing technical women in our field. And the fact that historically we haven't seen them at conferences is a cultural artifact that is not related to their lack of existence. And so, by creating diversity, and I think we don't have an... we don't only have a gender diversity problem. No. Diversity along many angles problem. But I think that the more that we create, we find these people. These people who are doing technically amazing work. And they've been in the industry for 5, 10, 20 years. And we celebrate their success. The more that we draw in people, and nobody should say, "Oh, I can't see anybody who looks like me. I don't belong here. " Right. I mean, the dream of technology is that it's a meritocracy, that it's a great equalizer. And it's just a terrible thing that's not actually happening. Right. And so that's what we're really trying to change. Anybody who says that women can't code never read about Grace Hopper. To me, it's utterly ridiculous. But I do want to thank you again for sitting down with me, and the work you're doing with the Browns Bridge Outreach. outreach. Thanks.

oral_history_curriculum.project: The Sound Above: UGtastic Technical Rewatch Series
oral_history_curriculum.historical_host_role: Senior Software Developer (2009-2015 recording era); Staff Software Engineer (modern identity)
oral_history_curriculum.launch_provenance: Officially launched on-site at SCNA 2011 (November 18-19, 2011 at Swissotel Chicago)

episodes.title: The First Room: Chicago Alt.NET & Practical Autonomy in Enterprise .NET
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who inspired the engineers breaking free from enterprise Microsoft silos? How did grassroots peer groups form before commercial developer platforms existed?
episodes.chicago_context: Chicago Alt.NET was the precursor room for dozens of Chicago developers who later founded startups, consultancy practices, and user groups.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Just as Alt.NET questioned monolithic enterprise frameworks, modern engineers must question monolithic cloud AI abstractions and reclaim local control.

episodes.title: The Ambassador: ChicagoRuby & Grassroots Hospitality
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who showed the early community organizers how to welcome newcomers with radical hospitality? What made ChicagoRuby a durable institution for two decades?
episodes.chicago_context: Ray Hightower served as the welcoming ambassador bridging corporate IT, independent consultants, and open-source practitioners.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: In an era of automated code synthesis, human hospitality and community mentorship become more valuable, not less.

episodes.title: Pair Friday in Libertyville: Apprenticeship & Terminal Workbenches
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who taught the 8th Light founders the discipline of apprenticeship? How did Carl Sagan and cosmic perspective shape their company philosophy?
episodes.chicago_context: 8th Light was founded in the Chicago suburbs, pioneering paid resident apprenticeships long before bootcamp pipelines existed.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Pair programming with an AI agent requires the exact same discipline as pairing with a junior apprentice: legible contracts, small steps, and continuous review.

episodes.title: The Apprenticeship Move: From Psychology to Craftsmanship
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who inspired Dave Hoover and Adewale Oshineye to write Apprenticeship Patterns? What can senior engineers learn from psychological mentorship models?
episodes.chicago_context: Dave Hoover helped lead Obtiva in Chicago, creating one of the earliest structured consultancy apprenticeship programs.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Apprenticeship Patterns ('Expose Your Ignorance', 'Deep Roots', 'Record What You Learn') are the antidote to shallow LLM copy-paste culture.

episodes.title: The 17-Year Continuous Room: Founding SCMC & Suburban Craftsmanship
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What sustained a monthly practitioner meetup in McHenry County for seventeen straight years without corporate sponsorship or speaker fees?
episodes.chicago_context: Mike Hall, Jim Suchy, and Ryan Gerry founded SCMC in spring 2009 following the Software Craftsmanship Manifesto, hosted at Follett and Panera Bread.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Grassroots community rooms provide psychological safety to test ideas, fail safely, and evaluate AI tooling with skeptical peer review.

episodes.title: Cranking Design to 11: Deliberate Practice & The Four Rules
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired Corey Haines to give away Coderetreat for free to the global community? How did Kent Beck's Four Rules of Simple Design become a physical, embodied practice?
episodes.chicago_context: Corey was an itinerant software craftsman traveling between Chicago, Cleveland, and international dojos, demonstrating that code design could be practiced like a martial art.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: When AI can generate an infinite volume of plausible code, constraint-based practice (no loops, no conditionals) is how humans retain structural judgment.
episodes.companion_video: Corey Haines: The Four Rules of Simple Design

episodes.title: The Toolmakers: Watir, WatiN & Automating the Browser
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who were the pioneers who proved that browser automation could be an open, developer-controlled test tool rather than expensive enterprise software?
episodes.chicago_context: SCNA corridor discussion connecting Watir (Ruby) and WatiN (.NET) maintainers, forming the foundation for modern web testing frameworks.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Modern agentic computer-use and browser automation tools are the direct descendants of the DOM-driving engines built in this era.

episodes.title: Clean Code in the Wild: Daily Practice & Object Mentor Wisdom
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired Tim Ottinger to co-author 'Clean Code' with Uncle Bob? What did Object Mentor learn from embedding directly on client teams across the Midwest?
episodes.chicago_context: Tim was a cornerstone mentor at Object Mentor in Gurnee/Libertyville, teaching practitioners the daily habits of refactoring and intention-revealing naming.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Naming things well is the primary interface between human programmers and LLMs. Meaningful names eliminate context-window ambiguity.
episodes.companion_video: Tim Ottinger: Meaningful Names in Practice

episodes.title: Cross-Pollination: Game Jams, Functional Code & Alt.NET
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who inspired Andrea to look beyond conventional business applications toward game development and functional programming? How did European and American developer communities cross-pollinate?
episodes.chicago_context: Andrea brought an international perspective to SCNA Chicago, showing how the Alt.NET ethos spread across Europe.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Siloed engineering leads to stagnation. Modern AI toolchains require cross-disciplinary curiosity across graphics, functional paradigms, and distributed data.

episodes.title: The Fast Feedback Loop: Destroy All Software & Unix Workbenches
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired Gary Bernhardt's obsession with sub-second feedback loops and terminal minimalism? How did 'WAT' and 'Destroy All Software' reshape an entire generation of developers?
episodes.chicago_context: Gary's legendary SCNA and RailsConf lightning talks and screencasts set the gold standard for terminal fluency and testing velocity in the Chicago developer community.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Fast feedback loops remain the ultimate competitive advantage. If your test suite takes 10 minutes to run, multi-agent iteration loops grind to a halt.

episodes.title: Questioning Orthodoxy: Tooling Empathy, Mocking & Human Consulting
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired Justin Searls to challenge dogma in test-driven development? How did Test Double pioneer a humane, empathetic model of consulting that prioritized team health over rigid doctrine?
episodes.chicago_context: Justin Searls was a major recurring voice at SCNA Chicago, using sharp humor and deep empathy to help developers laugh at their own architectural excesses.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Dogma is the enemy of effectiveness. As AI enters the software lifecycle, blindly applying 2010 testing rituals without understanding their purpose creates brittle friction.
episodes.companion_video: Justin Searls: Sometimes a Controller is Just a Controller

episodes.title: A Legacy of Learning: Community Hospitality, RailsBridge & In Memoriam
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What does it take to make a room full of strangers feel like a community where you belong? How do we build technical spaces that welcome those who have never seen a terminal?
episodes.chicago_context: Ginny Hendry was the quiet, generous heart of ChicagoRuby and 8th Light. Transitioning from decades of Fortran and systems engineering into Ruby, she organized and taught Chicago RailsBridge workshops and launched hands-on hack nights downtown, leaving an enduring legacy of learning after her 2017 passing.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Technical knowledge becomes obsolete rapidly; the human capacity to show up patiently, learn continuously, and teach others is the only permanent craft.
episodes.companion_video: 8th Light In Memoriam Tribute: Ginny Hendry, A Legacy of Learning

episodes.title: Hold Yourself to a Standard, But Let There Be Joy: Overcoming Developer Shame
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Why does the pursuit of technical excellence so often produce self-mockery and shame instead of joy? How do we replace hero worship with genuine empathy for people doing their best?
episodes.chicago_context: Leon Gersing brought a disarming, radical message of empathy and vulnerability to SCNA 2012, challenging the elitism of the conference circuit and reminding engineers that software is a third of their lives.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: As developers grapple with existential anxiety around automated code synthesis, Leon's message remains foundational: we are alive, we define our standard, let there be joy in solving problems.

episodes.title: Architecting the Open Door: RailsBridge & DevChix
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who taught Sarah Allen and Desi McAdam that the lack of diversity in tech was an educational pipeline problem that could be solved with open-source curricula?
episodes.chicago_context: Sarah Allen and Desi McAdam brought the RailsBridge movement to Chicago, partnering with local craft firms to run free weekend workshops that brought hundreds of women into programming.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Open-source educational curricula and zero-barrier installation scripts remain the model for democratizing access to complex emerging technology.

episodes.title: The Bridge Between Design and Craft: Girl Develop It Chicago
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired Jen Myers to bridge the cultural divide between visual designers and software craftsmen? How did Girl Develop It create safe spaces for adult learners in Chicago?
episodes.chicago_context: Jen Myers was a leading voice in Chicago tech, speaking at SCNA on why craftsmanship must include user experience, empathy, and welcoming adult career changers.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Software without user empathy is dead machinery. In an AI world, user experience design and humane interaction design matter more than raw backend plumbing.
episodes.companion_video: Jen Myers: Women in Technology and Design

episodes.title: Software as Communication: BDD, Humility & Deliberate Discovery
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who inspired Dan North to challenge dogma? Why did he refuse to monetize or certify Behavior-Driven Development?
episodes.chicago_context: Dan North's keynote at SCNA 2013 reframed craftsmanship from rigid rules to human communication and business empathy.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: 'Deliberate discovery' assumes ignorance is our constraint. Modern AI prompts fail when they assume certainty; humility yields better architectures.

episodes.title: Unlearning Dogma: From Snowbird 2001 to Elixir & Modern Craft
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired the original Pragmatic Programmer when writing with Andy Hunt in 1999? What led him to challenge Agile commercialization?
episodes.chicago_context: PragDave delivered one of the most provocative keynotes at SCNA Chicago, challenging attendees not to turn craftsmanship into a cult.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Rules that hardened twenty years ago must be re-evaluated. The spirit of the Pragmatic Programmer is experimentation, not orthodoxy.
episodes.companion_video: Dave Thomas: Agile is Dead (Long Live Agility)

episodes.title: The Truck Driver's Wisdom: Developer Humility & Tooling Craft
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who showed Hadi Hariri that software engineers are not special snowflakes? Why does empathy for real-world workers matter in systems design?
episodes.chicago_context: Hadi represented JetBrains at Chicago conferences, arguing for ergonomic IDEs that empower developers without arrogance.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Software engineers must remember they are toolsmiths serving human needs, especially as AI generates the boilerplate.
episodes.companion_video: Hadi Hariri: Refactoring to Functional Style

episodes.title: Speaking as Service: First-Time Speakers & Community Growth
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: How do technical conferences cultivate new voices? What does it take for junior practitioners to step onto the stage?
episodes.chicago_context: Sarah Gray shared her journey as a new conference speaker at SCNA 2013, highlighting the mentorship that made Chicago conferences welcoming.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Public speaking and sharing authentic case studies are how engineers build peer trust in a world flooded with synthetic content.

episodes.title: Deliberate Code Practice: Exercism, Feedback Loops & Refactoring
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired Katrina Owen to build Exercism.io? How does thoughtful, asynchronous mentorship transform beginners into confident craftsmen?
episodes.chicago_context: Katrina's talks and Exercism platform swept through Chicago user groups, establishing daily coding katas and empathetic code review as standard practice.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Mentorship is not just pointing out errors; it is asking guiding questions. Effective AI collaboration requires the same Socratic review mindset.

episodes.title: Developers and Depression: Mental Health in the Hallway Track
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired Greg Baugues to stand up before thousands of developers and break the silence around ADHD, bipolar, and mental health in software engineering?
episodes.chicago_context: Greg was a Chicago developer advocate, organizer, and former 8th Light apprentice whose landmark talk at RailsConf Chicago created the most impactful corridor conversation in conference history.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Neurodiversity is a core reality of engineering teams. Sustainable pacing, psychological safety, and honest vulnerability remain human responsibilities no model can replace.

episodes.title: The Craftsman's Social Contract: Artis & Inclusive Engineering
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What led Coraline Ada Ehmke to author the Contributor Covenant? How did early Chicago software craft debates connect to ethical open-source governance?
episodes.chicago_context: Coraline was a Chicago developer, writer, and speaker active in local user groups, arguing that technical craftsmanship cannot be separated from interpersonal ethics.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Ethical contracts and guardrails are mandatory when governing autonomous agentic behaviors across shared codebases.
episodes.companion_video: Coraline Ada Ehmke: The Myth of the 10x Developer

episodes.title: The Apprenticeship Lineage: Co-Authoring Apprenticeship Patterns
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Who were the mentors who shaped Ade Oshineye? What did he learn across Google and international software communities about passing the torch to the next generation?
episodes.chicago_context: Ade traveled to SCNA Chicago to share the foundational lessons of 'Apprenticeship Patterns', co-authored with Dave Hoover.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Apprenticeship is how unspoken tacit knowledge survives technological interregnums. When models generate solutions, understanding 'why' requires human lineage.
episodes.companion_video: Ade Oshineye: The Long Road to Mastery

episodes.title: The Chicago Corridor: Software as Writing & The TDD Debate
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired DHH's literary conception of software as writing? What sparked his 'TDD is Dead' keynote at the Chicago Sheraton?
episodes.chicago_context: RailsConf 2014 in Chicago was the epicenter of the debate between pragmatic product velocity and strict architectural dogma, debated in corridors with Martin Fowler and Uncle Bob.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Software architecture is not a math proof; it is prose meant for human understanding. Clarity and taste matter more than dogmatic ceremony.

episodes.title: Joy, Levity, and Systems Engineering: The Core Team Perspective
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: How did Aaron Patterson combine world-class Ruby C-extension and compiler optimization with playful humor and approachability?
episodes.chicago_context: Aaron Patterson's keynotes at RailsConf Chicago packed auditoriums, showing that deep systems performance does not require solemn pretense.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Deep runtime understanding (garbage collection, memory allocation, execution graphs) is what separates senior systems architects from passive prompt engineers.

episodes.title: Client-Side Architecture: Conventions, Shared State & The Ember Move
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired Yehuda Katz and Tom Dale to bring Rails-style strong conventions and router architecture to client-side JavaScript?
episodes.chicago_context: Recorded at RailsConf Chicago, this interview captures the moment frontend engineering moved from ad-hoc jQuery scripts into rigorous architectural frameworks.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Convention over configuration provides deterministic structure that makes autonomous code generation reliable and maintainable.
episodes.companion_video: Tom Dale & Yehuda Katz: The Future of the Web

episodes.title: Simple Made Easy: State, Time & Deconstructing Complexity
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What led Rich Hickey to spend two years in self-funded isolation designing Clojure? What is the profound difference between 'simple' and 'easy'?
episodes.chicago_context: Rich Hickey's talks and Clojure philosophy electrified Chicago craftsmanship groups, prompting practitioners to question mutability and object-oriented complexity.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Simplicity is an objective quality: unbraiding concerns. Easy is familiar. AI makes complex things easy to generate, making intentional simplicity vital.

episodes.title: The Reality of Legacy: Rewriting Software & Real-World Engineering Leadership
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired Camille Fournier's pragmatic approach to distributed systems at Rent the Runway? What does it actually take to rewrite production systems without killing the business?
episodes.chicago_context: Camille brought senior engineering leadership and architectural reality to GOTO Chicago, grounding distributed theory in production operations.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Legacy modernization is the defining challenge of modern software engineering. Autonomous agents must work inside living enterprise topologies, not empty greenfields.

episodes.era_name: The AI Horizon & The Observable Control Plane
episodes.title: The Living Document: Authorship, Provenance & Tech Media Evolution
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What happened to the physical technical book? How does knowledge preservation change when documentation becomes dynamic and digital?
episodes.chicago_context: Jason's WebVisions conversation captured the transition from print publishing to living web platforms.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: In an era of disposable synthetic code, living documentation and verified provenance are the anchors that prevent historical amnesia.

episodes.era_name: The AI Horizon & The Observable Control Plane
episodes.title: Community Self-Governance: Meta Sites, Moderation & Developer Communities
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: How do large-scale technical communities self-govern without authoritarian collapse? What role do meta feedback loops play in setting norms for millions of programmers?
episodes.chicago_context: Recorded during Adam Lear's tenure as Community Manager at Stack Exchange, exploring community governance models that outlast individual maintainers.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Autonomous multi-agent ecosystems require verifiable governance, clear moderation rules, and self-correcting mechanisms exactly like human communities.

episodes.era_name: The AI Horizon & The Observable Control Plane
episodes.title: Filling the Vessel: Performance, Craft & Clean Coders
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What does a craftsman owe an audience? How did the author of Clean Code think about teaching, performance, and professionalism?
episodes.chicago_context: Recorded at SCNA 2012 in Chicago while Uncle Bob was building the Clean Coders video series.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: When a model can emit code instantly, professionalism shifts to what we refuse to ship. The standards he taught are the review bar for generated code.

episodes.era_name: The AI Horizon & The Observable Control Plane
episodes.title: Extreme Programming Pioneers: Visual Thinking & Agile Without Dogma
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: What inspired the original XP signatories when they looked at the craftsmanship movement? How did Chet Hendrickson and Ron Jeffries maintain radical clarity amidst commercialization?
episodes.chicago_context: Chet Hendrickson and Ron Jeffries brought first-generation Extreme Programming lineage directly into SCNA 2013 dialogue.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: XP practices (continuous integration, small releases, relentless refactoring) are the essential guardrails that prevent autonomous agent loops from running amok.

episodes.era_name: The AI Horizon & The Observable Control Plane
episodes.title: Simplicity, Immutability & Datomic: Rethinking Information Architecture
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: Why did Clojure and Datomic capture the imagination of Midwest craftsmen seeking refuge from object-oriented ceremonies?
episodes.chicago_context: Stuart Halloway's SCNA presence connected the Chicago craftsmanship community with the emerging functional programming renaissance.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Immutable append-only facts and temporal event logs are the foundation of observable agent telemetries and memory layers.

episodes.era_name: The AI Horizon & The Observable Control Plane
episodes.title: Scaling Craftsmanship: The London Software Craftsmanship Community
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: How did the Chicago movement inspire transatlantic sister communities? What made the London Software Craftsmanship Community scale language-agnostically?
episodes.chicago_context: Sandro traveled from London to Chicago for SCNA 2012, solidifying the global network of craftsmanship communities.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Engineering craftsmanship is not an American or European idiom; it is a universal human discipline that crosses tool boundaries.

episodes.era_name: The AI Horizon & The Observable Control Plane
episodes.title: The Legacy Code Whisperer: Agile Technical Coaching & Sustainable Systems
episodes.sound_above_inquiry: How do technical coaches help legacy enterprise teams safely refactor critical codebases without despair?
episodes.chicago_context: Amitai was an integral voice across Chicago meetups and SCNA hallway conversations, championing gentle, persistent craftsmanship adoption.
episodes.ai_era_parallel: Modern AI engineering is fundamentally legacy engineering: making sense of existing complex codebases and wrapping them in automated safety nets.

nodes.label: Aspect-Oriented Programming
nodes.description: A way to describe behavior that crosses many parts of a program, then apply it at selected boundaries.

nodes.label: pointcut
nodes.description: The rule that selects the places in a program where an aspect is allowed to run.

nodes.label: join point
nodes.description: A meaningful moment in execution, such as entering a method, leaving it, or handling an error.

nodes.label: advice
nodes.description: The behavior an aspect runs at a selected join point, often before, after, or when an error occurs.

nodes.label: instrumentation
nodes.description: Adding measurements or signals to a system so its behavior can be observed while it runs.

nodes.label: OpenTelemetry
nodes.description: An open standard and set of tools for producing traces, metrics, and logs that describe system behavior.

nodes.label: Strangler Fig pattern
nodes.description: An incremental migration approach that routes one capability at a time to a new system while the old system remains useful.

nodes.label: Conway's Law
nodes.description: The systems an organization builds tend to reflect the communication paths through which the organization works.

nodes.label: Reverse Conway Maneuver
nodes.description: Shaping team boundaries and communication paths so the system that emerges has the architecture the organization needs.

nodes.label: Golden Signals
nodes.description: Four useful starting measures for service health: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.

nodes.label: service-level objective
nodes.description: A target for a measurable service outcome, including the boundary where the system is too hot or too cold.

nodes.label: System Cartography
nodes.description: A disciplined way to map a living system across code, runtime behavior, ownership, and organizational context before changing it.

nodes.label: Software Craftsmanship
nodes.description: A practitioner discipline grounded in simple design, test-driven feedback loops, apprenticeship, and care for how software is built and maintained.

nodes.label: command palette
nodes.description: A keyboard-driven interface for navigating pages, searching concepts, and inspecting relationships without leaving the keyboard.

nodes.label: knowledge work
nodes.description: Deliberate technical investigation that preserves context, provenance, and shared understanding across tools and time.

nodes.label: orientation
nodes.description: Establishing where you are in a system and what evidence is trustworthy before choosing an intervention.

nodes.label: Blindsight (Peter Watts)
nodes.description: Peter Watts' 2006 exploration of intelligence without consciousness and the Chinese Room thought experiment, illustrating the illusion of competence where complex symbol mapping operates without comprehension.

nodes.label: Looking Through the Net (Alan Watts)
nodes.description: Alan Watts' 1969 presentation to IBM systems engineers warning against mistaking conceptual nets, coordinate systems, and discrete tokens for the continuous reality they measure, contrasting mechanisms with living organisms and balancing analytical precision ('prickles') with organic holism ('goo').

nodes.label: Chinese Room thought experiment
nodes.description: John Searle's 1980 thought experiment demonstrating that syntactic symbol manipulation, no matter how sophisticated or convincing, does not constitute semantic understanding or consciousness.

nodes.label: The Mirage of Competence
nodes.description: The deceptive perception of understanding produced when a statistical model generates fluent, authoritative domain artifacts without causal grounding or sovereign verification.

nodes.label: AOP as the Bridge Between OpenTelemetry and the Strangler Fig
nodes.description: A field lesson on how Aspect-Oriented Programming makes cross-cutting behavior visible, supports OpenTelemetry, and helps teams find safer seams for incremental modernization.

nodes.label: AOP's Uses, Misuses, and Boundaries
nodes.description: When Aspect-Oriented Programming clarifies a system, when it hides control flow, and how to choose a boundary without creating invisible behavior.

nodes.label: From Fiverr to whisper.cpp: Building a Verifiable Oral History Pipeline
nodes.description: The long path from expensive, lossy outsourced transcription to a local, resumable, human-reviewed pipeline for preserving technical conversations.

nodes.label: A Simple Ruby Block as an AOP-Shaped Boundary
nodes.description: A small Ruby example showing how a block can make before, operation, exit, and error behavior explicit at a reusable boundary.

nodes.label: The Archive I Could Finally Build
nodes.description: What UGtastic, Dead Rabbit Radio, the Fluffle transcription experiment, Raspberry Pi processing, and local AI taught me about preserving oral history.

nodes.label: The Shortcut That Shifts Toward Knowledge
nodes.description: A small keyboard gesture as a reminder to slow down, orient, and move deliberately toward knowledge.

nodes.label: What Aspect-Oriented Programming Is
nodes.description: A plain-language introduction to aspects, join points, pointcuts, advice, and cross-cutting concerns, grounded in Mike Hall's PostSharp work.

nodes.label: The Mirage of Competence: AI Slop & Domain Boundaries
nodes.description: A practitioner inquiry into AI slop, domain boundaries, and forensic audio recovery under 345kV power lines, examining what it means to practice human craftsmanship when AI tools project effortless confidence.

patreon_campaign.purpose: Independent compute underwriting, oral history preservation, and humanizing the people who make tech communities, user groups, and open-source software possible.
patreon_campaign.manifesto: Supporting WHOIS Tech Community will bring you more interviews with fascinating people with higher production quality. I'll be able to spread the interviews across a larger swathe of communities and bring you a better understanding and awareness of the cool people in tech. I believe in the life changing value of tech community and know how much work goes into even small user-groups and conferences as well as OSS projects. Most of the people creating and coordinating these works are working behind the scenes and often go unrecognized. I seek these people out and put them in front of a camera to learn more about what they are doing and why they are doing it. My goal is to help with humanizing and increasing awareness of the cool people who make tech community possible. Since 2011 I've conducted over 200 interviews with tech leaders both famous and not so famous. I've learned a lot about the equipment and interviewing techniques and the interviews have slowly been improving both technically and content-wise. I need help though to grow past the current state. Going to conferences and collecting the equipment has been quite expensive and I want to avoid advertising entanglements. I want WHOIS Tech Community to be 100% focused on people doing cool stuff without worrying about which tool or vendor I need to please. If you support WHOIS Tech Community then you will help me to purchase better equipment that will lead to higher production values for interviews. I will be able to spend more time on developing the WHOISTechCmty.com website to build better profiles and interesting ways to promote individuals in tech community. And most importantly I'll be able to dedicate more time to seeking out and interviewing fascinating people in tech. This will help you to learn about the people who are in your community that you might not even be aware of.
